claims.text: Resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation in HEA multilayer coatings arises from synergy between intralayer lattice distortion or short-range order and nanoscale interfaces.
Interfaces between dissimilar HEA layers are strong barriers to dislocation nucleation.
Interfaces between dissimilar HEA layers impede dislocation transmission.
The multilayer interfaces impede both dislocation glide and climb during creep.
Alternating nanoscale HEA layers can be made slightly compositionally or structurally distinct while retaining an overall high-entropy matrix.
Sputtering or hot isostatic pressing can produce the proposed high-density heterointerface multilayer coating architecture.
A homogeneous single-phase HEA coating with equivalent overall composition is an appropriate control for isolating the effect of the multilayer architecture.
Constant-stress tests at 600–800 °C over extended durations will capture time-dependent creep deformation in the proposed coatings.
Multilayer interfaces generate local misfit strains and alter chemical short-range order.
The resulting interface network pins dislocations and increases the energy barrier for transmission across layers.
Chemical short-range order within an HEA can reduce dislocation mobility.
Intrinsic lattice distortion within each layer reduces dislocation mobility.
Changes in composition or ordering at interlayer boundaries force approaching dislocations to bow or acquire additional activation energy.
Combining intralayer and interfacial barriers reduces creep strain and creep rate over time.
Under identical high-temperature creep conditions, a multilayer HEA coating will have lower creep strain and a slower strain rate than a homogeneous coating of the same overall composition.
The mechanism is expected to operate for layer thicknesses in the tens-of-nanometers range and below roughly 0.5 Tm, where dislocation-mediated creep dominates.
Porosity, excessive processing defects, or large compositional gradients can confound the effect attributed to interfaces.
The relative contributions of lattice distortion and interfacial barriers may vary with alloy chemistry, layer thickness, and processing-induced residual stress.
